newsitem.title: UK: Stoiber says EMU delay better than weak euro.
newsitem.headline: Stoiber says EMU delay better than weak euro.

text.p: A delay in Europe's Economic and Monetary Union would be better than a weak single currency, Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, said in a newspaper published on Monday.
"A controlled delay would certainly be better than a weak European currency," Stoiber told the Financial Times. "It would mean holding to the goal of the euro and holding firm to the criteria."
In this way, EMU could perhaps start "on January 1, 2000 or 2001," the newspaper quoted him as saying.
Stoiber said he was an absolute supporter of a stable euro but the Maastricht criteria must be strictly interpreted, including the three percent deficit to GDP target.

"If for five years we say that the euro will be as stable as the D-mark, that the criteria must be strictly applied, that the criteria have precedence over the timetable and if a year before January 1, 1999, we suddenly start saying the opposite, then as far as I'm concerned we lose our competence to govern -- and not just as far as the euro is concerned but in many other areas," he said.
He said unlike in the U.S., the euro area will have no single financial policy, no single tax policy, no single economic policy and all member states will retain their full sovereignty and autonomy.
For that reason, "we need certain binding criteria to make the results of the differing policies comparable," he said.
Stoiber said in the interview that the EMU stability pact has three percent as its upper limit for deficit-to- GDP.

"From 1999, any country exceeding three percent must in principle pay a penalty," he said. "You can't join a club by observing rules that are less stringent than those that apply in the club," he said.

The newspaper said Stoiber made clear he expected Germany's European Union partners to meet the 3.0 percent criterion. He said Germany must give an evaluation next year about the stability of other countries.
"That means -- leaving aside any exceptional factors -- that we will not have 3.0 percent for one, 3.5 percent for another and 3.8 percent for yet another." REUTER
